        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your own CI/CD pipeline).  
I’ll also give you the exact file contents you’ll need to create/modify so you can paste them straight into the repo.

> ⚠️ **Important** – I don’t have the ability to run `git` or `docker` commands from here, but the commands below are ready‑to‑run on a machine that has `git`, `docker`, and `kubectl` installed.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you’re in the directory where you want the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you already have a local copy, just pull the latest changes:

```bash
cd nodejs-welcome
git pull origin main
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick scan to see what the repo contains:

```bash
tree -L 2   # shows top‑level directories/files
cat package.json   # look at dependencies, scripts, start command
```

Typical findings for a Node.js “welcome” app:

| File | Typical content |
|------|-----------------|
| `app.js` | Express server listening on `process.env.PORT || 3000` |
| `package.json` | `"start": "node app.js"` |
| `.env.example` | Example env vars |

> If the repo uses a different entry point (`index.js`, `server.js`, etc.) adjust the Dockerfile accordingly.

### 2.2 Create / update `Dockerfile`

Create a new file named `Dockerfile` (no extension) in the repo root with the following content:

```Dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install dependencies first (cached layer)
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Build step (if needed; skip if not required)
# RUN npm run build

# Runtime stage
FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy only built artifacts + node_modules
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app .

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *Why this Dockerfile?*  
> • Uses multi‑stage build to keep the image small.  
> • Installs production deps only (`npm ci --only=production`).  
> • Exposes port 3000 (adjust if your app uses another port).

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (create the `k8s` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: nodejs-welcome-secrets   # optional: load secrets
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # change to NodePort/ClusterIP as needed
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # service port
    targetPort: 3000  # container port
```

> *What to tweak:*  
> • Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with your Docker registry URL (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq`).  
> • Add environment variables via `env:` or `envFrom:` if your app needs them.  

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # needed for ghcr.io

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ hashFiles('**/Dockerfile') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
        cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache-new

    - name: Move cache
      run: |
        rm -rf /tmp/.buildx-cache
        mv /tmp/.buildx-cache-new /tmp/.buildx-cache
```

> *Key points:*  
> • Uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication (no extra secrets needed).  
> • Caches Docker layers to speed up subsequent builds.  
> • Tags the image as `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome:latest`.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

If you want to see what’s staged:

```bash
git status
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the next push to `main`.  
> You should see the workflow run under the **Actions** tab of the repo.

---

## Quick sanity check

Once the workflow finishes successfully:

1. Verify the image exists in GHCR (or your chosen registry).
2. Apply the Kubernetes manifests locally or in your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

3. Check pod status:

```bash
kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome
```

4. Port‑forward to test:

```bash
kubectl port-forward svc/nodejs-welcome-service 8080:80
curl http://localhost:8080
```

You should receive the expected response from your Node.js app.

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

- A production‑ready Dockerfile  
- Kubernetes deployment & service YAMLs  
- A fully‑functional GitHub Actions workflow that builds & pushes on every push to `main`  

Feel free to tweak the replica count, service type, or image registry as your environment requires. Happy deploying!
